beseech.gloss: To beg someone urgently and humbly for something; formal and literary in modern American English.

senses.head: Beg urgently, implore
senses.body: Formal and literary; in ordinary speech Americans beg or plead instead. The regular past *beseeched* is now more common in American writing than *besought*.
examples: The families *beseech* the governor to reopen the case.
Her lawyers *besought* the judge for one more week.
Advocates *have besought* the agency for years to publish the data.

senses.head: Entreat in prayer or older prose
senses.body: The scriptural and literary register, where *besought* is the expected past. You meet it in translations, hymns, and historical fiction rather than in speech.
examples: The pilgrims *besought* heaven for rain.
He *had besought* his father to forgive him before the old man died.
In the last chapter she *beseeches* the reader to remember her kindly.

bring.gloss: To carry or take someone or something to the place where you are or are going; also, to cause a result or a state.

senses.head: Carry or take to this place
senses.body: The motion is toward the speaker or toward the place being talked about. If the movement is away from you, the verb is *take*.
examples: Please *bring* your ID to the appointment.
She *brought* dessert to the potluck.
Somebody *has brought* a dog into the lobby.

senses.head: Cause a state or result
senses.body: The subject produces the effect, and the object is usually abstract: rain, joy, trouble, publicity, change.
examples: Spring *brings* the tourists back.
The merger *brought* three years of chaos.
That decision *has brought* nothing but lawsuits.

senses.head: Bring about (cause to happen)
senses.body: A fixed phrase for making a change actually happen, often after effort or delay.
examples: It took a strike to *bring about* a new contract.
Their reporting *brought about* the resignation.
Technology *has brought about* changes nobody planned for.

senses.head: Bring up (raise a topic)
senses.body: To introduce a subject into a conversation, often one others would rather avoid.
examples: Don't *bring up* the layoffs at dinner.
She *brought up* the budget again.
Nobody *has brought* it *up* since the meeting.

senses.head: Bring up (raise a child)
senses.body: Common in both countries, though Americans often prefer *raise*. Frequently passive: *he was brought up in Ohio*.
examples: He was *brought up* by his grandmother.
They *brought up* four kids on one salary.
She *has brought up* two children alone.

senses.head: Bring in (earn or recruit)
senses.body: Two everyday uses: money that a business takes in, and a person hired or called in from outside.
examples: The store *brings in* about six thousand a week.
They *brought in* a consultant after the second outage.
We *have brought in* two new engineers this quarter.

senses.head: Bring down (topple or reduce)
senses.body: Used both of removing someone from power and of lowering a number such as a price, a fever, or a rate.
examples: The scandal *brought down* the mayor.
Nothing will *bring down* a fever that fast.
Generic drugs *have brought* prices *down* sharply.

senses.head: Bring oneself to (force oneself)
senses.body: Almost always negative or with *can't*: you are unable to make yourself do something painful.
examples: I can't *bring* myself to sell the house.
She never *brought* herself to apologize.
He *has* never *brought* himself to watch the tape.

senses.head: Bring charges, bring a suit
senses.body: The standard legal collocation for starting a case against someone.
examples: Prosecutors may still *bring* charges.
The tenants *brought* a class action.
The state *has brought* three cases against the company.

buy.gloss: To get something by paying money for it; informally, also to believe something or to gain it at a cost.

senses.head: Purchase, pay money for
senses.body: The core sense. Keep it apart from *brought*, the past of *bring*: money makes it *bought*.
examples: We *buy* our vegetables at the farmers market.
He *bought* the truck used, with ninety thousand miles on it.
They *have bought* a house outside Tucson.

senses.head: Believe, accept as true
senses.body: Informal, and usually negative: *I don't buy it*. The object is a story, an excuse, or an argument.
examples: I don't *buy* that excuse.
The jury never *bought* his story.
Nobody *has bought* that line since the first press conference.

senses.head: Gain at a cost
senses.body: What is paid is not always money; the object is often time, silence, safety, or goodwill.
examples: The delay *bought* us two more weeks.
A second server would *buy* some breathing room.
That concession *has bought* them nothing at all.

senses.head: Bribe, buy off
senses.body: Informal but unambiguous. With *off* it means paying someone to drop an objection or a claim.
examples: You cannot *buy* a federal judge.
The company *bought off* two inspectors.
Someone *had bought* his silence long before the hearing.

senses.head: Buy into (accept, or take a stake)
senses.body: Either to be persuaded by an idea or to purchase a share of a business. The context separates them.
examples: Half the team never *bought into* the new process.
She *bought into* the partnership in 2019.
Investors *have bought into* the story completely.

senses.head: Buy out (purchase someone's share)
senses.body: To acquire the whole of another party's stake so they leave the business.
examples: His brothers *bought* him *out*.
They offered to *buy* her *out* at book value.
A private equity firm *has bought out* the chain.

catch.gloss: To take hold of something moving, and by extension to capture, reach in time, notice, or contract something.

senses.head: Seize something moving
senses.body: The literal sense: stop an object in flight with your hands.
examples: Dogs *catch* frisbees better than most people do.
She *caught* the glass before it hit the floor.
The goalie *has caught* everything they have thrown at him.

senses.head: Capture, trap
senses.body: Of animals, fish, or people who are running from you.
examples: Traps rarely *catch* anything this time of year.
We *caught* three fish and threw them all back.
Police *have caught* the driver.

senses.head: Discover someone in the act
senses.body: Normally *catch someone doing something*, with an -ing form and never an infinitive.
examples: He *caught* his roommate going through his mail.
Don't let them *catch* you parking there.
Two managers *have* been *caught* falsifying the logs.

senses.head: Be in time for
senses.body: Of trains, flights, the end of a movie, or a person before they leave.
examples: If I run I can *catch* the 6:40.
She *caught* the last train out of the city.
We *have caught* that flight twice with ten minutes to spare.

senses.head: Contract an illness
senses.body: Used of infections you pick up from other people, not of chronic conditions.
examples: Kids *catch* everything in their first year of school.
He *caught* a cold the week before the wedding.
She *has caught* the flu twice this winter.

senses.head: Hear or understand
senses.body: Usually negative or in an apology: *I didn't catch that*.
examples: I didn't *catch* your last name.
He *caught* only half of what she said over the noise.
Nobody *has caught* the joke yet.

senses.head: Notice, spot a mistake
senses.body: Of errors, discrepancies, and problems found before they do damage.
examples: Spellcheck *catches* the obvious ones.
She *caught* the discrepancy on the second read.
An intern *has caught* two errors the auditors missed.

senses.head: Snag, become stuck
senses.body: The subject is the thing that snags, and the phrase is normally *catch on* something.
examples: The zipper *catches* about halfway up.
My sleeve *caught* on the door handle.
A branch *had caught* the kite ten feet up.

senses.head: Catch up (reach the same point)
senses.body: Of distance, of work left undone, or of news between friends who have not talked in a while.
examples: Go ahead; I'll *catch up*.
He *caught up* on email over the weekend.
We *have caught up* on the backlog at last.

senses.head: Catch on (become popular; understand)
senses.body: Two settled meanings: a fashion or a name spreads, or a person finally grasps what is going on.
examples: The name never *caught on*.
She *caught on* faster than anyone expected.
The style *has caught on* with younger buyers.

creep.gloss: To move slowly, quietly, and low to the ground, or to advance by small degrees.

senses.head: Move slowly and stealthily
senses.body: Quiet movement meant to go unnoticed, often close to the ground.
examples: Don't *creep* around behind me like that.
The cat *crept* along the fence rail.
He *had crept* downstairs before anyone else woke.

senses.head: Advance by small degrees
senses.body: Figurative, usually with *up* or *in*: costs, delays, doubts, and errors creep rather than jump.
examples: Doubt *creeps* in around three in the morning.
A little sarcasm *crept* into her emails.
Costs *have crept* up about four percent this year.

senses.head: Grow along a surface
senses.body: Of ivy, vines, and moss; the adjective *creeping* names whole plant families.
examples: Ivy will *creep* up the north wall if you let it.
Moss *crept* over the stones.
The vine *has crept* across the whole trellis.

senses.head: Creep up on (approach unnoticed)
senses.body: Of a person sneaking up, and just as often of a date or a season arriving before you noticed.
examples: Winter *crept up on* us.
She *creeps up on* you with the sad part of the song.
The deadline *has crept up on* everyone.

senses.head: Creep someone out
senses.body: Informal, and the one use of this verb with a regular past: *that movie creeped me out*, never *crept me out*.
examples: That mask *creeps* me out.
The whole basement *creeped* us out.
His messages *have creeped* her out for weeks.

daydream.gloss: To let your mind wander to pleasant imaginary things while you are awake.

senses.head: Drift off, stop paying attention
senses.body: No object: the point is the lapse of attention rather than what you imagine. American English uses *daydreamed*; *daydreamt* reads as British.
examples: I *daydream* through most of the Monday status call.
He *daydreamed* his way through an hour of the lecture.
My son *has daydreamed* through two years of algebra.

senses.head: Daydream about (imagine what you want)
senses.body: With *about* or *of*. What follows is a wish rather than a plan, which is what separates it from *plan* or *intend*.
examples: I *daydream* about a week with no phone.
She *daydreamed* about quitting for the whole drive home.
They *have daydreamed* about opening a bakery for years.

deal.gloss: To handle or cope with something, to hand out playing cards, or to trade in goods.

senses.head: Deal with (handle, cope with)
senses.body: The everyday sense, always with *with*. The object is a problem, a complaint, or a difficult person.
examples: I *deal with* vendor complaints all morning.
He *dealt with* the same landlord for six years.
The agency *has dealt with* worse crises than this one.

senses.head: Hand out playing cards
senses.body: The card-table sense, and the source of the noun *dealer* and of *a raw deal*.
examples: *Deal* me in.
She *dealt* the cards and we started playing.
The house *has dealt* him four bad hands in a row.

senses.head: Deal in (trade in, sell)
senses.body: Of a business and the goods it handles. Also figurative: a paper that *deals in* rumor.
examples: The shop *deals in* rare maps.
His family *dealt in* grain for a century.
They *have dealt in* used equipment since the eighties.

senses.head: Sell illegal drugs
senses.body: Informal, and usually with no object at all: *he got caught dealing*.
examples: You do not *deal* on that corner without permission.
Two of them *dealt* out of the same apartment.
She *has* never *dealt* anything harder than weed.

senses.head: Deal a blow, deal out
senses.body: Somewhat formal. The object is a blow, damage, justice, or the hand that fate gives you.
examples: Judges *deal out* the same sentence for both offenses.
The ruling *dealt* a blow to the plaintiffs.
Life *has dealt* him a bad hand this year.

senses.head: Deal with (be about)
senses.body: Of books, chapters, reports, and laws: what the text covers.
examples: Chapter four *deals with* the war years.
The report *dealt with* only one of the three sites.
Nobody *has dealt with* the legal side in print.

dream.gloss: To see images and stories while asleep, or to imagine something you badly want.

senses.head: See images while asleep
senses.body: With *about* or *of*. English makes the sleeper the subject, so Russian *мне снилось* becomes *I dreamed*. American English writes *dreamed*; *dreamt* is British and sounds poetic here.
examples: I rarely *dream* about work.
She *dreamed* about her grandmother's house again.
He *has dreamed* the same thing three nights running.

senses.head: Wish for, aspire to
senses.body: With *of* or *about*, and often with *since* or *always* to show how long the wish has lasted.
examples: We *dream* of a year with no travel.
She *dreamed* of medical school and got there.
He *has dreamed* of playing at Carnegie Hall since he was six.

senses.head: Imagine as possible
senses.body: Almost always negative: *never dreamed*, *wouldn't dream of it*. The second is also a polite refusal.
examples: I wouldn't *dream* of asking her to pay.
She never *dreamed* it would take four years.
Nobody *had dreamed* the vote would be that close.

senses.head: Dream up (invent)
senses.body: Of a plan, a name, or an excuse, usually with a hint that it was invented too quickly.
examples: Marketing *dreams up* a new slogan every quarter.
Who *dreamed* this policy *up*?
We *had dreamed up* the whole plan over one dinner.

senses.head: Dream on (informal dismissal)
senses.body: A fixed imperative used to tell someone their hope is unrealistic. It appears in no other form.
examples: A corner office in year one? *Dream on*.
He thinks they'll double the offer. *Dream on*.

feel.gloss: To experience an emotion or a sensation, to touch something to learn about it, or to hold an impression or an opinion.

senses.head: Experience an emotion or state
senses.body: Followed by an adjective, not an adverb: *I feel bad*, not the adverb form.
examples: I *feel* better after a walk.
They *felt* ignored by management for months.
He *has felt* dizzy since the medication changed.

senses.head: Touch to examine
senses.body: Deliberate touching to find out about texture, temperature, or swelling.
examples: *Feel* how heavy this is.
She *felt* the fabric and put it back on the shelf.
The doctor *has felt* the swelling and ordered a scan.

senses.head: Perceive by sensation
senses.body: Here the stimulus comes from outside you: wind, a bump, a tremor, pain.
examples: Can you *feel* the draft from that window?
We *felt* the tremor an hour before the news reported it.
I *have* not *felt* my toes since mile eight.

senses.head: Seem, give an impression
senses.body: The subject is a thing or a place rather than a person, and it takes an adjective: *the room feels cold*.
examples: The room *feels* colder than the thermostat says.
The whole meeting *felt* rehearsed.
This draft *has felt* wrong from page one.

senses.head: Hold an opinion
senses.body: Softer than *think*: a judgment offered as personal rather than argued.
examples: I *feel* we should wait a week.
She *felt* the price was too high.
The board *has felt* that way since the audit.

senses.head: Feel like (want, be in the mood for)
senses.body: Followed by a noun or an -ing form, never an infinitive: *feel like leaving*, not *feel like to leave*.
examples: I *feel like* pizza.
Nobody *felt like* driving another three hours.
She *has* not *felt like* going out since the move.

senses.head: Feel for (sympathize with)
senses.body: Fellow feeling for someone in trouble. Do not confuse it with *feel up*, which is something else entirely.
examples: I *feel for* anyone flying today.
We all *felt for* him after the news.
She *has felt for* those families from the start.

senses.head: Feel up to (be well enough for)
senses.ru: быть в состоянии, чувствовать в себе силы
senses.body: Mostly in questions and negatives, about energy or health rather than ability.
examples: Do you *feel up to* a walk?
He didn't *feel up to* the drive.
She *has* not *felt up to* company all week.

senses.head: Feel out (probe cautiously)
senses.body: To test someone's position quietly before committing to a proposal.
examples: *Feel* them *out* before you name a number.
We *felt out* two other vendors.
He *has* already *felt out* the committee.

keep.gloss: To go on having something, to store it somewhere, or to make someone or something stay in a state.

senses.head: Continue to have, retain
senses.body: The opposite of giving something back or throwing it away.
examples: *Keep* the change.
He *kept* every letter she sent him.
They *have kept* the same phone number since 1998.

senses.head: Store in a place
senses.body: Where a thing lives when it is not in use; usually with a place phrase.
examples: We *keep* the extra keys in the kitchen drawer.
She *kept* the deed in a safe-deposit box.
The store *has kept* my measurements on file.

senses.head: Cause to stay in a state
senses.body: Takes an object plus an adjective, a participle, or a place: *keep the door open*, *keep them waiting*.
examples: *Keep* the door open.
The noise *kept* us awake.
That heater *has kept* the shop warm all winter.

senses.head: Keep doing (continue)
senses.body: Always with an -ing form, never an infinitive: *keep trying*, not *keep to try*. *Keep on* is the emphatic version.
examples: My landlord *keeps* raising the rent.
He *kept* apologizing until it got awkward.
She *has kept* asking the same question for a month.

senses.head: Observe, fulfill, hold to
senses.body: The object is a promise, an appointment, a secret, a schedule, or a law.
examples: He *keeps* his promises.
She *kept* the news to herself all week.
They *have* not *kept* a single appointment this month.

senses.head: Look after, support, maintain
senses.body: Of animals, gardens, records, or a household you pay for. This is the sense behind *earn your keep*.
examples: They *keep* chickens and two goats.
He *kept* a family of five on a machinist's wage.
The parish *has kept* records since 1830.

senses.head: Stay fresh, last
senses.body: No object, and mostly of food. Figuratively, news that *will keep* can wait until later.
examples: Hard cheese *keeps* for months.
The soup *kept* fine in the freezer.
Whatever it is *has kept* this long, so it can wait until Monday.

senses.head: Keep up (maintain a pace or standard)
senses.body: Either matching someone else's speed or continuing something at the same level.
examples: I can't *keep up* with the reading.
He *kept up* with the leaders for ten miles.
They *have kept up* the payments without a single miss.

senses.head: Keep from, keep off (prevent)
senses.body: *Keep someone from* doing something is preventing it; *keep off* keeps a thing away.
examples: *Keep* him *from* signing anything today.
She *kept* herself *from* laughing.
The tarp *has kept* the rain *off* the woodpile.

senses.head: Keep to (stick to, stay within)
senses.body: Of a schedule, a route, a budget, or a routine. *Keep to yourself* is a separate fixed phrase meaning to stay private.
examples: *Keep to* the schedule.
We *kept to* the main road.
He *has kept to* the same routine for twenty years.

kneel.gloss: To go down on your knees, or to stay in that position.

senses.head: Go down on your knees
senses.ru: опуститься на колени, встать на колени
senses.body: Both pasts are standard American English: *knelt* is usual in edited prose, *kneeled* in sports and news writing. The k is silent in every form.
examples: You have to *kneel* to see the bottom shelf.
He *knelt* to tie his son's shoe.
She *has knelt* on that hard floor for an hour.

senses.head: Kneel in prayer or reverence
senses.body: The religious use, where *knelt* is strongly preferred.
examples: The ushers ask the congregation to *kneel* at that point in the service.
The pilgrims *knelt* on the stone steps.
They *have knelt* there every evening since the accident.

senses.head: Take a knee in protest
senses.ru: встать на одно колено в знак протеста
senses.body: A recent American use dating from the 2016 anthem protests; *kneeled* is the past you usually see in this context.
examples: Athletes still *kneel* at some events.
Several players *kneeled* during the anthem.
Half the team *had kneeled* before the anthem even started.

lean.gloss: To bend or rest your body or an object at an angle, and by extension to tend toward a position or rely on someone.

senses.head: Bend the body from upright
senses.body: Movement of your own body toward or away from something. American English uses *leaned*; *leant* is British and a homophone of *lent*.
examples: Don't *lean* out that far.
He *leaned* over the counter to read the sign.
She *has leaned* into the aisle to see the screen all game.

senses.head: Rest against a support
senses.body: Of a person or an object propped at an angle; also of a structure that has tilted and stayed that way.
examples: The old barn *leans* about two degrees to the east.
She *had leaned* her bike against the wrong tree.
The fence *has leaned* toward the road since the storm.

senses.head: Tend toward, be inclined
senses.body: With *toward*, or with *left* and *right* when the subject is a voter, a county, or a paper.
examples: The county *leans* Republican.
I *leaned* toward the cheaper option.
The committee *has leaned* that way from the start.

senses.head: Lean on (rely on, or pressure)
senses.body: Two meanings held apart by context: depending on someone for support, or, informally, coercing them.
examples: You can *lean on* me for the deposit.
His brother *leaned on* him to sell.
We *have leaned on* that one vendor too much this quarter.

senses.head: Lean in (commit, engage fully)
senses.body: Business slang of the last decade: to embrace something instead of hedging or apologizing for it.
examples: We should *lean in* rather than apologize.
The brand *leaned in* on the joke.
They *have leaned in* hard on video this year.

leap.gloss: To jump a long way or high, and by extension to rise sharply or to act suddenly.

senses.head: Jump far or high
senses.body: Both *leaped* /lipt/ and *leapt* /lɛpt/ are standard American, unlike *dreamt* and *leant*.
examples: Deer *leap* that fence every spring.
The cat *leapt* from the counter to the top of the fridge.
He *had leapt* out of the way just in time.

senses.head: Rise sharply (of numbers)
senses.body: Of prices, sales, rents, or stock, and always a sudden move rather than a steady climb.
examples: Rents *leap* every time a new building opens.
The stock *leapt* again on no real news.
Sales *have leaped* thirty percent since March.

senses.head: Leap at (act eagerly)
senses.body: Of an offer or a chance taken without hesitation. *Leap into* something carries a warning about haste.
examples: Don't *leap* into a lease you can't break.
She *leaped at* the chance to transfer.
He *has leaped at* every opening they have posted.

senses.head: Leap to conclusions
senses.body: A fixed phrase, always a criticism: judging before the facts are in.
examples: She *leaps* to conclusions faster than anyone I know.
The press *leapt* to the obvious conclusion.
We *have leaped* to the wrong one twice already.

leave.gloss: To go away from a place or a person, or to let something stay behind or stay in a condition.

senses.head: Go away, depart
senses.body: With or without an object: *leave the house*, *leave for Chicago*, or simply *leave*.
examples: We *leave* for the airport at six.
They *left* before the second act.
The train *leaves* from track nine.

senses.head: Quit for good
senses.body: Of a job, a school, a band, or a marriage, where the departure is permanent.
examples: Half the staff will *leave* if that policy stands.
She *left* him in the spring.
He *has left* the company after eleven years.

senses.head: Let something stay behind
senses.body: Covers both deliberate leaving and simple forgetting; a message left for someone belongs here too.
examples: Don't *leave* your laptop in the car.
She *left* her badge on her desk.
I *have left* you three voicemails.

senses.head: Cause to remain in a state
senses.body: Takes an object plus an adjective or a participle: *leave the door open*, *left us speechless*.
examples: *Leave* the light on.
The news *left* everyone speechless.
The flood *has left* two blocks without power.

senses.head: Bequeath
senses.body: Of property passed on at death, usually with an indirect object: *left her the cabin*.
examples: People rarely *leave* anything to a second cousin.
Her aunt *left* her the cabin.
He *has left* everything to the university.

senses.head: Entrust, delegate
senses.body: *Leave it to me*, or *leave something up to* someone: handing over responsibility for a decision.
examples: *Leave* it to me.
They *left* the wording to the lawyers.
We *have left* the scheduling up to her.

senses.head: Remain, be left over
senses.body: Normally the participle with *be*, and the standard way to state a remainder in arithmetic.
examples: There are two cookies *left*.
Six from ten *leaves* four.
Nothing was *left* of the barn but the foundation.

senses.head: Leave out (omit)
senses.body: Of information or people left off a list, whether by accident or on purpose.
examples: *Leave* the middle section *out*.
You *left out* the best part.
They *have left* two names *out* of the credits.

senses.head: Leave alone, leave behind
senses.body: *Leave alone* means stop bothering; *leave behind* means abandon or outpace.
examples: *Leave* her *alone*.
The team *left* him *behind* in free agency.
Growth *has left* the older neighborhoods *behind*.

lose.gloss: To stop having something, to be unable to find it, or to fail to win.

senses.head: Misplace, be unable to find
senses.body: Spelling trap: *lose* has one o and ends in /z/; *loose* is the adjective meaning not tight.
examples: I *lose* my glasses about twice a day.
She *lost* her keys somewhere between the car and the door.
He *had lost* the receipt, so the store refused the return.

senses.head: Fail to win
senses.body: Of games, elections, bets, and court cases. You lose *to* an opponent and lose *by* a margin.
examples: That team *loses* whenever it rains.
We *lost* the game in overtime.
They *have lost* four straight.

senses.head: Cease to have
senses.body: Of a job, weight, hair, a signal, or a reputation: something you had that is now gone.
examples: You *lose* the signal in that tunnel.
He *lost* his job in the second round of cuts.
She *has lost* twenty pounds since January.

senses.head: Be bereaved of
senses.body: The ordinary English way of saying someone died: *she lost her father*. Plain, not euphemistic.
examples: Nobody wants to *lose* a parent that young.
She *lost* her father last spring.
The town *has lost* three people to that road.

senses.head: Fail to keep control of
senses.body: With *control*, *your temper*, *track*, *patience*, *your nerve*: things that slip away rather than get misplaced.
examples: Try not to *lose* your nerve at the last minute.
He *lost* his temper in the meeting.
I *have lost* track of how many times we have filed this.

senses.head: Waste, fail to use
senses.body: Of time, money, and opportunities consumed with nothing to show for them.
examples: Every delay *loses* money.
We *lost* an hour to a bad merge.
The project *has lost* two months to review.

senses.head: Get rid of, shake off
senses.body: Informal: lose a pursuer, or lose something unwanted such as a jacket or an attitude.
examples: *Lose* the jacket; it's ninety degrees.
He *lost* them somewhere in the parking garage.
She *has lost* the accent almost completely.

senses.head: Be lost (astray, or not following)
senses.body: The participle behaves like an adjective, so *I am lost* is a state, not a past tense. It covers both losing your way and losing the thread of an explanation.
examples: We got *lost* twice on the way up.
You *lost* me at the second slide.
He *has lost* me completely with this explanation.

may.gloss: A modal verb expressing possibility or permission; *might* is its past form and also a weaker present possibility.

senses.head: Express possibility
senses.body: *May* states a real chance, *might* a slighter one. No -s, no -ing, and no *to* after either.
examples: The delay *may* push the launch to April.
She *might* come, but I doubt it.
The road *might* be closed by then.

senses.head: May have, might have (past possibility)
senses.body: To place a possibility in the past, use *may have* or *might have* plus a participle. There is no participle of *may* itself, so *have might* does not exist.
examples: He *might have* taken the earlier flight.
The package *may have* gone to the old address.
We *may have* met at a conference years ago.

senses.head: Grant or ask permission
senses.body: Formal register. In everyday American speech people use *can*; *may* survives in rules, notices, and polite questions.
examples: You *may* leave once the form is signed.
*May* I ask who's calling?
Students *may* not retake the exam.

senses.head: Might in reported speech
senses.body: This is where *might* still works as a true past: it is the backshifted form of *may* after a past reporting verb.
examples: She said we *might* need a second interview.
He told the class they *might* use their notes.
The letter said applicants *may* appeal within thirty days.

senses.head: Might as a tentative suggestion
senses.body: A softened recommendation, usually *you might want to* or *might as well*. Only the *might* form works this way.
examples: You *might* want to call ahead.
We *might* as well start without him.
She *might* try the other entrance.

senses.head: Concede a point
senses.body: Formal. *May* grants something before the sentence turns on it, normally with *but*.
examples: It *may* be legal, but it is a terrible idea.
He *may* have the votes; he does not have the money.
The design *may* look odd at first, and then it makes sense.

senses.head: Formal wish
senses.body: Ceremonial and literary, with *may* at the front of the clause and no subject inversion elsewhere.
examples: *May* you both be very happy.
*May* it please the court.

mean.gloss: To have a particular sense, to intend something, or to matter to someone.

senses.head: Signify, denote
senses.body: What a word, a sign, or a gesture stands for. The subject is the thing that carries the sense.
examples: What does this abbreviation *mean*?
The red light *meant* the door was locked.
That symbol *has meant* the same thing since the 1950s.

senses.head: Intend to do
senses.body: Followed by an infinitive. *I meant to* usually introduces an apology for not doing it.
examples: I don't *mean* to interrupt.
I *meant* to call you back yesterday.
We *have meant* to repaint this room for years.

senses.head: Intend a particular sense
senses.body: About the speaker's intent rather than the words: what you were trying to say or to do by saying it.
examples: What I *mean* is that we can't ship on Friday.
She *had meant* it as a compliment.
He *has* never *meant* anything by it.

senses.head: Entail, result in
senses.body: The subject is an event or a decision and the object is its consequence.
examples: A second round *means* another two weeks.
The merger *meant* layoffs in both offices.
That change *has meant* rewriting half the tests.

senses.head: Matter, have value to someone
senses.body: Always with *to* someone, and usually with a quantity: *means a lot*, *means nothing*.
examples: Your opinion *means* more to him than you think.
The award *meant* nothing to her.
That *has meant* a great deal to my family.

senses.head: Be meant for, be meant to
senses.body: Passive only. *Be meant for* is purpose or destiny; *be meant to* states what the rules or instructions require.
examples: This chair was *meant* for the hallway.
You are *meant* to sign both copies.
They were *meant* for each other.

outthink.gloss: To beat someone by thinking more cleverly than they do.

senses.head: Outsmart, outmaneuver mentally
senses.body: A prefixed *think*, inflecting exactly like it. Common in sports, chess, and negotiation.
examples: You can't *outthink* a machine at chess anymore.
Their defense *outthought* ours for four quarters.
She *has outthought* every negotiator they have sent.

senses.head: Outthink oneself
senses.body: Reflexive and always a criticism: you lose by choosing the clever answer over the obvious one.
examples: He *outthought* himself and passed on the obvious answer.
We *have outthought* ourselves on this design.

oversleep.gloss: To sleep longer than you meant to.

senses.head: Sleep past the time you meant to get up
senses.body: No object: you simply *oversleep*, never *oversleep your alarm*. It always implies the sleep was accidental, which is what separates it from *sleep in*.
examples: If I *oversleep*, start the meeting without me.
He *overslept* and missed his connection.
She *has overslept* twice this week.
They *had overslept*, so breakfast was already cleared away.
My roommate *oversleeps* every single Monday.

rethink.gloss: To think about something again in order to change your plan or your opinion.

senses.head: Reconsider a decision
senses.body: Of one choice, date, or answer, held up for a second look.
examples: We should *rethink* the launch date.
She *had rethought* her answer by the time she reached the door.
I *have rethought* my position on remote work.

senses.head: Redesign an approach
senses.body: Of a system, a policy, or a business model rather than a single decision. The noun shifts its stress to the first syllable: *the plan needs a rethink*.
examples: Every startup *rethinks* its pricing in year two.
The board *rethought* the whole budget in one afternoon.
They *have rethought* their return policy twice this year.

seek.gloss: To try to find or obtain something; formal in American English, where everyday speech says *look for*.

senses.head: Try to obtain
senses.body: The commonest American use, and mostly legal or official: you seek damages, asylum, a permit, approval, or office.
examples: Applicants may *seek* an extension in writing.
The company *sought* damages in federal court.
He *had sought* asylum twice before.

senses.head: Try to find, search for
senses.body: Formal or literary. In speech Americans *look for* their keys and *seek* only records, evidence, or shelter.
examples: Birds *seek* open water in a hard freeze.
Rescuers *sought* the hikers for three days.
Investigators *have sought* those records since May.

senses.head: Ask for advice or comment
senses.body: The object is what you request from another person: advice, comment, a second opinion, guidance.
examples: The paper *seeks* comment from both sides before publishing.
We *sought* a second opinion.
She *has sought* advice from three different lawyers.

senses.head: Seek to do (attempt)
senses.body: Formal written English with an infinitive. The plain equivalent is *try to*.
examples: The bill *seeks to* close that loophole.
The administration *sought to* limit the damage.
Plaintiffs *have sought to* reopen the case twice.

senses.head: Seek out (go and find deliberately)
senses.body: The particle adds effort and intent: you go looking for one specific person or thing.
examples: New employees should *seek out* a mentor.
He *sought out* the one person who had read the file.
She *has sought out* every recording he ever made.

senses.head: Sought-after (in demand)
senses.body: Only an adjective, built on the participle and normally placed before the noun.
examples: She is the most *sought-after* editor in town.
Those are the most *sought-after* seats in the building.

sleep.gloss: To rest with your eyes closed and your mind unconscious.

senses.head: Rest unconscious
senses.body: No object in this sense: *I slept badly*, not *I slept a bad night*.
examples: I *sleep* badly in hotels.
The baby *slept* through the whole flight.
He *has slept* on that couch for a month.

senses.head: Provide beds for
senses.body: The subject is a house, a boat, a tent, or a van, and the object is a number of people.
examples: The cabin *sleeps* six.
That rental *slept* eight comfortably.
The van *has slept* three of us on longer trips.

senses.head: Sleep in (stay in bed late)
senses.body: Deliberate and pleasant, which is exactly what separates it from *oversleep*.
examples: We *sleep in* on Sundays.
She *slept in* until noon.
I *have* not *slept in* since the baby came.

senses.head: Sleep on it (postpone a decision)
senses.body: A fixed phrase: wait a night before answering so you can think it over.
examples: *Sleep on it* and tell me tomorrow.
They *slept on* the offer and countered Monday.
We *have slept on* worse decisions than this one.

senses.head: Sleep with (have sex with)
senses.body: A polite euphemism that fools nobody. *Sleep together* is the reciprocal form.
examples: Everyone assumed they *had slept* together.
She *slept with* his best friend and told him herself.
Half the plot turns on who *sleeps with* whom.

senses.head: Sleep off (recover by sleeping)
senses.body: Of jet lag, a hangover, or a long flight; the object goes between the verb and the particle when it is a pronoun.
examples: *Sleep* it *off* and call me in the morning.
He *slept off* the jet lag on the couch.
She *has slept off* worse hangovers than that.

sweep.gloss: To clean a floor with a broom, or to move something (or move yourself) in a broad, forceful arc.

senses.head: Clean with a broom
senses.body: The literal sense. Americans *sweep up* a room; the verb *upsweep* is not used for cleaning.
examples: I *sweep* the porch every Saturday.
He *swept* the broken glass into a dustpan.
Nobody *has swept* the shop floor in a week.

senses.head: Push or clear away in one motion
senses.body: One broad arm movement that clears a surface, with no broom involved.
examples: *Sweep* the crumbs onto a plate.
She *swept* the papers off the desk into a box.
Wind *had swept* the leaves into one corner of the yard.

senses.head: Move powerfully across a place
senses.body: Of fire, storms, disease, rumor, or a political movement covering everything in its path.
examples: A cold front *sweeps* down the valley every March.
The fire *swept* through the canyon in an afternoon.
Rumors *have swept* the office all week.

senses.head: Move with grand, unhurried motion
senses.body: Of a person entering or leaving a room. Slightly literary and often ironic.
examples: She *sweeps* into a room like she owns it.
He *swept* past the receptionist without a word.
They *have swept* out of two meetings this month.

senses.head: Win everything
senses.body: American sports and awards usage: take every game in a series or every category on the night.
examples: No one expected them to *sweep* the series.
Their film *swept* the technical categories.
The team *has swept* all four games.

senses.head: Search or scan systematically
senses.body: Of security teams, searchlights, and radar: covering an area in a steady pattern.
examples: Searchlights *sweep* the fence line every few minutes.
Security *swept* the room for bugs.
Crews *have swept* both floors twice.

senses.head: Sweep under the rug, sweep aside
senses.body: Fixed phrases for hiding something embarrassing or brushing off an objection.
examples: He *sweeps aside* every objection.
The complaint got *swept* under the rug.
They *have swept* two investigations under the rug.

teach.gloss: To give someone knowledge or a skill.

senses.head: Instruct someone in something
senses.body: English splits what Russian *учить* covers with one verb: the teacher *teaches* and the student *learns*, so *she learned me algebra* is wrong.
examples: Can you *teach* a beginner in a month?
She *taught* me algebra in one weekend.
He *has taught* himself three languages.

senses.head: Work as a teacher
senses.body: With a subject, a grade, or a place, and often with no object at all: *she teaches*.
examples: I *teach* two sections of writing in the fall.
She *taught* fourth grade for thirty years.
They *had taught* the course together before the merger.

senses.head: Cause someone to learn from experience
senses.body: The subject is an event or an experience rather than a person.
examples: One bad winter *teaches* you to keep chains in the trunk.
The recall *taught* the company nothing.
That experience *has taught* me to read the contract first.

senses.head: Teach someone a lesson
senses.body: Informal and punitive: a threat or a boast about punishment, not real instruction.
examples: That fine will *teach* him a lesson.
She *taught* them a lesson they still talk about.
Two audits *have taught* the department to file on time.

think.gloss: To use your mind to consider something, or to hold an opinion about it.

senses.head: Hold an opinion, believe
senses.body: The commonest use, normally with a *that* clause. In the negative, English moves the *not* onto *think*: *I don't think he's coming*.
examples: I *think* we should wait a week.
She *thought* the meeting was on Thursday.
We *had thought* the issue was fixed.

senses.head: Use the mind, reason
senses.body: No object: the activity itself. This is the sense in *let me think* and *think straight*.
examples: Let me *think*.
He *thought* for a long moment before answering.
I *have* not *thought* clearly since four this morning.

senses.head: Think about (consider)
senses.body: Turning something over in your mind, often over a long period.
examples: *Think about* what you're asking her to do.
We *thought about* moving to Denver.
He *has thought about* applying for years.

senses.head: Think of (recall or come up with)
senses.body: Retrieving a name or producing an idea on the spot. Often negative: *I can't think of his name*.
examples: I can't *think of* her last name.
She *thought of* three objections right away.
Nobody *has thought of* a better title.

senses.head: Intend, be considering
senses.body: Usually in the progressive, *be thinking of* plus an -ing form, which makes a plan sound tentative.
examples: I was *thinking* of leaving early.
We *think* we'll drive instead of flying.
They *had thought* they would be home by now.

senses.head: Think through, think over
senses.body: *Think through* means follow the consequences all the way; *think over* means take time before answering.
examples: *Think* it *over* and call me Monday.
She *thought* the whole plan through in one night.
They *have thought* this through more carefully than we have.

senses.head: Think up (invent)
senses.body: Of a name, an excuse, or a scheme, with a hint that it was made up quickly.
examples: He *thinks up* a new excuse every week.
Who *thought up* this schedule?
They *have thought up* three names and hate all of them.

senses.head: Think of as, think highly of
senses.ru: относиться как к, быть высокого мнения
senses.body: How you rate someone or what category you put them in.
examples: Her professors *think* highly of her.
We *thought of* him as a friend.
The industry *has* always *thought of* the company as a follower.

senses.head: Think twice, think better of
senses.body: Fixed phrases: *think twice* warns before the act, *think better of it* reports a change of mind after it.
examples: *Think twice* before you sign that.
He *thought better of* it and stayed home.
She *has* never *thought twice* about telling the truth.

upsweep.gloss: To sweep or curve something upward; you will meet it mostly as the participle *upswept*.

senses.head: Arrange hair upward
senses.body: Rare as a verb; the adjective *upswept* and the noun *an upsweep* are far more common. For cleaning a room Americans say *sweep up*, never *upsweep*.
examples: The stylist can *upsweep* your hair for the ceremony.
She *upswept* her hair and pinned it with a tortoiseshell comb.
By seven she *had upswept* every loose strand.

senses.head: Curve upward
senses.body: Design and engineering vocabulary: *upswept wingtips*, *upswept tail fins*, an *upswept* shoulder line.
examples: That silhouette *upsweeps* sharply at the shoulder.
The designers *have upswept* the tail fins on the new model.
Wind *has upswept* the snow into a ridge along the roofline.

weep.gloss: To cry, especially quietly and from deep feeling; literary in American English.

senses.head: Cry from deep feeling
senses.body: Literary. In everyday American English people *cry*; *weep* raises the register or the seriousness.
examples: Some people *weep* at weddings and some at airports.
She *wept* when she read the letter.
He *has wept* only twice in his adult life.

senses.head: Ooze liquid slowly
senses.body: Of a wound, a pipe, a joint, or a valve losing liquid a drop at a time. Same irregular past.
examples: The old radiator *weeps* a little onto the floor.
The cut *wept* for two days.
That valve *has wept* since the day they installed it.

senses.head: Weep for, weep over (mourn)
senses.body: Formal, with *for* or *over*, and often ironic in the negative: nobody will weep for a bank.
examples: Nobody is going to *weep for* a bank.
The whole family *wept* through the service.
Historians *have wept over* the loss of that archive for two centuries.

wreak.gloss: To cause a great deal of damage or trouble; in practice almost always *wreak havoc*.

senses.head: Wreak havoc, wreak damage
senses.body: The modern past is *wreaked*. *Wrought* is historically the past of *work*, not of *wreak*, so American English writes *wreaked havoc*.
examples: A late frost can *wreak* havoc on the orchards.
The hurricane *wreaked* damage along sixty miles of coast.
Budget cuts *have wreaked* havoc on the department.

senses.head: Wreak vengeance
senses.body: Formal and literary. The object is revenge, vengeance, or someone's anger, and it falls *on* or *upon* a target.
examples: He *wreaked* his revenge slowly and in public.
The gods *had wreaked* their anger on the city.
No rival *has wreaked* vengeance that publicly in years.
